items.title: Global temperature, 1880–2025 (from NASA data)
items.description: Each year from 1880 to 2025 becomes one note, taken from NASA's measured global temperature record. NASA's map animation of the same record plays in step above a chart with one colored stripe per year (blue for cooler than the 1951–1980 average, red for warmer) and a line tracing the values.
items.summary: For the first sixty years the notes stay low and wander. From about 1980 they climb steadily, and the last decade holds the highest notes of the whole piece. The warmest year in the record is 2024.

keyMoments.text: 1880: the record begins, slightly below the 1951–1980 average.
1909: the coldest year in the record, about 0.48 °C below the average. This is the lowest note.
1944: a warm peak in the 1940s, about 0.20 °C above the average.
1964: a brief dip to about 0.20 °C below the average.
1980: the steady climb begins. Most notes from here are higher than the ones before.
1998: a sharp jump to about 0.61 °C above the average during a strong El Niño.
2016: the first year more than 1 °C above the average.
2024: the warmest year in the record, about 1.28 °C above the average. This is the highest note.

about.heading: How it is measured
about.text: NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies combines air temperatures from thousands of weather stations on land with sea surface temperatures from ships and buoys. Each value is an anomaly: the difference from the 1951–1980 average.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.text: The global average is the most widely used single measure of how much the planet has warmed.

items.title: Global temperature month by month, 1880–2026 (from NASA data)
items.description: Every month from January 1880 to October 2026, from NASA's global temperature record, compared with the 1951–1980 average. A continuous tone follows the monthly value, and two plucked notes mark each year, in January and in July.
items.summary: The yearly version of this record sounds like a steady climb. Month by month it is restless: the tone jitters constantly, because single months swing by several tenths of a degree. Under the jitter the same climb is there. The last month colder than the 1951–1980 average was September 1992. A month first reached 1 °C above that average in January 2007, and every month since June 2023 has been at least 1 °C above it. The highest month in the record is the most recent one, October 2026, at about 1.55 °C.

keyMoments.text: January 1880: the record begins.
January 1893: the coldest month in the record, about 0.81 °C below the average.
September 1992: the last month colder than the 1951–1980 average.
January 2007: a month reaches 1 °C above the average for the first time.
February 2016: about 1.36 °C above the average, during a strong El Niño.
May 2023: the last month less than 1 °C above the average.
October 2026: the warmest month in the record, about 1.55 °C above the average.

items.title: Arctic temperature, 1880–2025 (from NASA data)
items.description: Each year from 1880 to 2025 becomes one note, taken from NASA's temperature record for the Arctic, the region north of 64° latitude. Values are compared with the 1951–1980 average. The chart shows one colored stripe per year with a line tracing the values.
items.summary: The Arctic swings far more from year to year than the planet as a whole, so the notes leap around. There is a cold stretch in the 1880s, a warm spell around 1940, a cooler dip in the 1960s, and then a steep climb from the 1990s. Over the last ten years the Arctic averaged about 2.6 °C above its 1951–1980 level, roughly two and a half times the global figure of about 1.0 °C.

keyMoments.text: 1887: the coldest year in the record, about 1.73 °C below the average. This is the lowest note.
1938: the peak of an early warm spell, about 1.52 °C above the average.
1966: a cold dip, about 0.76 °C below the average.
1992: the last year colder than the 1951–1980 average.
2005: the first year at least 2 °C above the average.
2016: the warmest year in the record, about 3.23 °C above the average. This is the highest note.
2025: the record ends at about 2.93 °C above the average, the second-warmest year.

about.text: The same NASA analysis as the global record, averaged over the region north of 64° latitude.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.text: The Arctic is warming faster than the planet as a whole, which affects sea ice, frozen ground and the Greenland ice sheet.

items.title: Compare: the Arctic against the whole planet (from NASA data)
items.description: Two NASA temperature records play at once on the same pitch scale: the Arctic (north of 64° latitude) in your left ear and the whole planet in your right ear. Because the scale is shared, you can hear directly how far apart they are.
items.summary: For the first century the left ear leaps about while the right ear barely moves: the Arctic swings by more than a degree from year to year and the planet does not. From about 1990 the left ear pulls away upward. In 34 of the 36 years since 1990 the Arctic was further above its 1951–1980 average than the planet was. Over 2016–2025 the Arctic averaged about 2.6 °C above that average, against about 1.0 °C for the planet.

keyMoments.text: 1887: the Arctic's coldest year, about 1.73 °C below average, while the planet was 0.36 °C below.
1938: an Arctic warm spell, about 1.52 °C above average, while the planet was at its average.
2004: the last year the Arctic was not further above its average than the planet.
2016: the widest gap. The Arctic was about 3.23 °C above average and the planet 1.01 °C.
2025: the Arctic at about 2.93 °C above average, the planet at 1.19 °C.

items.title: Compare: north half against south half of the planet (from NASA data)
items.description: Two NASA temperature records play at once on the same pitch scale: the Northern Hemisphere in your left ear and the Southern Hemisphere in your right ear.
items.summary: For a century the two ears stay close together, and from 1950 to 1985 the south was the further above its average in 19 of the 36 years. Since 1996 the north has been ahead every year and the gap has widened. Over 2016–2025 the north averaged about 1.29 °C above its 1951–1980 average and the south about 0.73 °C. The north has more land, and land warms faster than ocean.

keyMoments.text: 1996: the last year the Southern Hemisphere was further above its average than the Northern.
1998: the Southern Hemisphere first reaches 0.5 °C above its average.
2015: the Northern Hemisphere first reaches 1 °C above its average.
2024: the warmest year for both. The north was about 1.65 °C above average and the south 0.92 °C.

items.title: Carbon dioxide in the air, 1959–2025 (from NOAA data)
items.description: Each year from 1959 to 2025 becomes one note, taken from the yearly average amount of carbon dioxide in the air measured at Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii, in parts per million. The chart shows one colored stripe per year with a line tracing the values.
items.summary: The notes only ever go up. Carbon dioxide rises every single year in the record, from about 316 parts per million in 1959 to about 427 in 2025. The climb also gets steeper: about 0.9 parts per million a year in the 1960s, and about 2.6 a year over the last ten years. A brighter, sharper tone marks the years with the biggest jumps.

keyMoments.text: 1959: the first full year of measurements, about 316 parts per million. This is the lowest note.
1988: carbon dioxide passes 350 parts per million.
2015: carbon dioxide passes 400 parts per million.
2023: carbon dioxide passes 420 parts per million.
2024: the largest one-year rise in the record, about 3.5 parts per million.
2025: about 427 parts per million, the highest in the record. This is the highest note.

about.heading: How it is measured
about.text: Air is sampled continuously at Mauna Loa Observatory, high on a volcano in Hawaii and far from cities and forests. Measurements began there in 1958, making this the longest continuous record of carbon dioxide in the air.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.text: Carbon dioxide traps heat. Its rise is the main cause of the warming heard in the temperature items.

items.title: The planet breathing: carbon dioxide month by month, 1958–2026 (from NOAA data)
items.description: Every month from March 1958 to September 2026, from the carbon dioxide record at Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii. A continuous tone follows the monthly value. Two plucked notes mark each year: one in May, when carbon dioxide peaks, and one in September, when it is near its yearly low.
items.summary: You hear a wobble riding on a climb. Each year carbon dioxide rises to a peak in May, then falls by about 6 parts per million to a low in September or October, as plants across the Northern Hemisphere grow through the summer and take carbon dioxide out of the air. Through autumn and winter it rises again. The wobble has stayed about the same size, but each year's low is higher than the last. The monthly value first reached 400 parts per million in May 2013, and no month has been below 400 since November 2015.

keyMoments.text: March 1958: the record begins at about 315.7 parts per million.
October 1958: the lowest month in the whole record, about 312.4 parts per million.
May 1986: a month reaches 350 parts per million for the first time.
May 2013: a month reaches 400 parts per million for the first time.
October 2015: the last month below 400 parts per million.
April 2022: a month reaches 420 parts per million for the first time.
May 2026: the highest month in the record, about 432.3 parts per million.

about.text: Air is sampled continuously at Mauna Loa Observatory, high on a volcano in Hawaii and far from cities and forests. Measurements began there in 1958.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.text: The yearly wobble is the living world at work: most of Earth's land plants are in the Northern Hemisphere, and their summer growth draws carbon dioxide down. The climb underneath it is the part that people have added.

items.title: Methane in the air, 1984–2025 (from NOAA data)
items.description: Each year from 1984 to 2025 becomes one note, taken from the worldwide yearly average of methane in the air, in parts per billion.
items.summary: This one has a plot twist. The notes climb quickly through the 1980s, slow down in the 1990s, and then almost stop: from 1999 to 2006 methane hardly changed, and in three of those years it fell slightly. In 2007 the climb starts again. It reaches its fastest pace in 2021 and 2022, about 16 parts per billion a year, and has slowed a little since. Methane rose from about 1,645 parts per billion in 1984 to about 1,936 in 2025.

keyMoments.text: 1984: the record begins at about 1,645 parts per billion. This is the lowest note.
1999: the rise stalls. For the next seven years methane hardly changes.
2005: the largest one-year fall in the record, about 2.9 parts per billion.
2007: the rise starts again, about 6.4 parts per billion in one year.
2011: methane passes 1,800 parts per billion.
2022: the largest one-year rise, about 16.1 parts per billion, and methane passes 1,900.
2025: about 1,936 parts per billion, the highest in the record. This is the highest note.

about.heading: How it is measured
about.text: Air samples are collected at a worldwide network of remote sites at sea level and averaged into one global figure.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.text: Methane is the second most important greenhouse gas from human activity. Each molecule traps far more heat than carbon dioxide, but it lasts only about a decade in the air.

items.title: Heat stored in the ocean, 2005–2025 (from NOAA data)
items.description: Each year from 2005 to 2025 becomes one note, taken from NOAA's estimate of the heat stored in the top 2,000 metres of the world's oceans. Values are in units of ten billion trillion joules, compared with NOAA's long-term reference level.
items.summary: A short record with a simple shape: up. The notes rise in 18 of the 20 steps and dip only in 2007 and 2016. By 2025 the ocean holds about 22 more units of heat than it did in 2005, taking the figure from about 10 to about 33, roughly three times as far above the reference level.

keyMoments.text: 2005: the record begins at about 10.2 units. This is the lowest note.
2016: the larger of the two dips, a fall of about 1.6 units.
2017: the largest one-year rise, about 2.8 units.
2025: about 32.5 units, the highest in the record. This is the highest note.

about.heading: How it is measured
about.text: Thousands of drifting robotic floats, called Argo floats, dive to 2,000 metres and measure temperature on the way back up. They have covered the world's oceans since the mid-2000s, which is why this record starts in 2005.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.text: The ocean takes up about nine-tenths of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases. That heat raises sea level, because warm water expands, and it feeds marine heatwaves.

items.title: Arctic sea ice in September, 1979–2026 (from satellite data)
items.description: Each year from 1979 to 2026 becomes one note, taken from the satellite record of how much of the Arctic Ocean is covered by sea ice in September, the month when the ice is at its smallest. Values are in millions of square kilometres. The chart shows one colored stripe per year with a line tracing the values.
items.summary: Here a falling note means less ice. The notes start high and drift down for twenty years, drop sharply in 2007, and hit the lowest note in 2012. Since then they have stayed low without falling further. September ice averaged about 7.2 million square kilometres in the first ten years of the record and about 4.6 million in the last ten, a loss of more than a third.

keyMoments.text: 1980: the most September ice in the record, about 7.67 million square kilometres. This is the highest note.
1996: the last year close to the early levels, about 7.58 million square kilometres.
2003: the last September with more than 6 million square kilometres of ice.
2007: a sharp drop to about 4.27 million square kilometres.
2012: the least September ice in the record, about 3.57 million square kilometres. This is the lowest note.
2020: the second-lowest year, about 4.00 million square kilometres.
2026: the record ends at about 4.81 million square kilometres.

visual.caption: A chart with one stripe per year. Blue stripes are years with more ice and red stripes are years with less; the line and the label show the same values, so nothing depends on color alone.

about.heading: How it is measured
about.text: Satellites carrying microwave sensors have mapped sea ice continuously since late 1978. They work through cloud and through the polar night. Extent is the area of ocean with at least 15% ice cover.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.text: Bright ice reflects sunlight and dark open water absorbs it, so less summer ice means the Arctic Ocean takes up more heat.

items.title: Compare: Arctic sea ice in winter and in summer, 1979–2026 (from satellite data)
items.description: Two records play at once on the same pitch scale: Arctic sea ice in March, when it reaches its winter peak, in your left ear, and in September, at its summer low, in your right ear. More ice is a higher note.
items.summary: The left ear stays high and the right ear stays low, because there is always far more ice in winter. Listen to how each one moves. The winter notes drift down gently: March ice averaged about 15.9 million square kilometres in the first ten years and about 14.5 million in the last ten, a loss of about a tenth. The summer notes fall much further: from about 7.2 million to about 4.6 million, a loss of more than a third. The ice still grows back each winter, but less of it survives each summer.

keyMoments.text: 1979: the record begins with the most March ice in the record, about 16.34 million square kilometres, and 7.05 million in September.
2007: September ice drops sharply to about 4.27 million square kilometres.
2012: the least September ice in the record, about 3.57 million square kilometres.
2025: the least March ice in the record, about 14.12 million square kilometres.

visual.caption: A chart with one stripe per year, colored by the March value. The solid line is March and the dashed line is September; the label shows both values.

timbre.explain: More ice sounds brighter. The right-ear record also has a slightly buzzier tone so the two are easy to tell apart.

about.heading: How it is measured
about.text: Satellites carrying microwave sensors have mapped sea ice continuously since late 1978. Extent is the area of ocean with at least 15% ice cover.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.text: Ice that survives the summer becomes thicker, older ice. As less survives, more of the Arctic's ice is thin first-year ice that melts easily the next summer.

items.title: Antarctic sea ice in February, 1979–2026 (from satellite data)
items.description: Each year from 1979 to 2026 becomes one note, taken from the satellite record of sea ice around Antarctica in February, the end of the southern summer, when the ice is at its smallest. Values are in millions of square kilometres.
items.summary: Listen to this after the Arctic item, because it behaves differently. For more than thirty-five years the notes bounce up and down with no downward drift, and some of the highest notes come late: 2008 is the highest, and 2013 to 2015 are almost as high. Then the floor drops. February ice falls sharply in 2016 and 2017, and 2022 and 2023 set new record lows. February ice averaged about 3.1 million square kilometres from 1979 to 2015 and about 2.5 million from 2017 to 2026. The last note, 2026, is back up near 2.9 million.

keyMoments.text: 1979: the record begins at about 3.14 million square kilometres.
2008: the most February ice in the record, about 3.89 million square kilometres. This is the highest note.
2015: the last of three high years in a row, about 3.80 million square kilometres.
2017: a sharp drop to about 2.29 million square kilometres, a record low at the time.
2023: the least February ice in the record, about 1.98 million square kilometres. This is the lowest note.
2026: a partial recovery to about 2.91 million square kilometres.

about.text: Unlike the Arctic, Antarctic sea ice showed no long-term decline for most of the satellite record. Scientists are still working out what caused the sudden drop after 2015 and whether it will last.

items.title: The Antarctic ozone hole, 1979–2025 (from NASA data)
items.description: Each year from 1979 to 2025 becomes one note, taken from NASA's record of the size of the ozone hole over Antarctica. The value is the hole's average area between 7 September and 13 October, when it is at its largest, in millions of square kilometres.
items.summary: This is the one record here with a turn in it. The hole barely exists in 1979, then grows through the 1980s, year after year, to more than 20 million square kilometres by 1992. It stays large, with the largest in 2006. Since then the notes have stopped climbing and begun, unevenly, to come down: the hole averaged about 23 million square kilometres from 1998 to 2008 and about 20 million from 2016 to 2025. Two years stand far below their neighbours, 2002 and 2019, when unusual weather high over Antarctica broke the hole up early.

keyMoments.text: 1979: almost no hole, about 0.1 million square kilometres. This is the lowest note.
1987: the hole reaches about 19.3 million square kilometres. This is the year the world agreed the Montreal Protocol to phase out the chemicals that cause it.
1992: the hole passes 20 million square kilometres for the first time.
2002: a sudden small year, about 12.0 million square kilometres, caused by unusual weather high over Antarctica.
2006: the largest hole in the record, about 26.6 million square kilometres. This is the highest note.
2019: about 9.3 million square kilometres, the smallest since 1983, again because of unusual weather.
2025: about 18.7 million square kilometres.

about.heading: How it is measured
about.text: NASA and NOAA satellites have measured ozone over Antarctica every year since 1979. The hole is the area where ozone falls below 220 Dobson units.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.text: Ozone high in the atmosphere blocks ultraviolet light from the Sun. The hole was caused by chemicals once used in fridges and spray cans. Countries agreed to phase them out, and the ozone layer is slowly recovering: it is the clearest case of the world fixing a planet-wide environmental problem.

items.title: Spread of the Dixie Fire, 2021 (from NASA frames)
items.description: NASA's animation of the Dixie Fire in California from 14 July to 22 October 2021, updated every 12 hours from satellite fire detections. Yellow lines mark recent fire fronts (the newest is brightest), red dots mark active fire detections, and grey shading shows the total area burned. A graph on screen tracks the cumulative burned area. The sound is computed live from the colors of each frame.
items.summary: The fire begins as a small patch in mid-July. Through late July and early August the grey burned area spreads quickly across the map while the view pulls back to keep it in frame. In mid-August active fire is burning along the northern and eastern edges. From September the red detections become few, and by 30 September none are visible; the graph of burned area has levelled off. The final frame overlays the outlines of all the earlier fire fronts.

items.title: Ocean surface currents and temperature, 2007–2008 (from NASA frames)
items.description: NASA's animation of global sea surface currents from 25 March 2007 to 3 March 2008. The flow lines are colored by sea surface temperature: blue for 0 °C, through green and yellow, to red for 32 °C. The sound is computed live from the colors of each frame.
items.summary: A flat map of the world's oceans, with land in grey. Swirling flow lines cover the water: red and orange along the tropics where the sea is warmest, green and yellow at middle latitudes, and blue near the poles. Over the year the pattern changes gently. The warm band strengthens and weakens, and the reddest water shifts between the western Pacific, the Indian Ocean and the tropical Atlantic.

items.title: Lightning seen from the Space Station, 2017–2023 (from NASA frames)
items.description: NASA's animation of lightning detected by the Lightning Imaging Sensor on the International Space Station from January 2017 through July 2023. A moving 10-day window brings out the seasonal pattern. The sound is computed live from the colors of each frame.
items.summary: The animation begins on 1 March 2017, following the Space Station's track across a dark Earth as the first flashes appear as yellow dots. It then shows the whole globe slowly turning while a 10-day window moves through the years to 2023. Yellow dots gather thickly over land in the tropics, especially central Africa, South America and south-east Asia, and thin out over the open ocean. The clusters shift north and south with the seasons.
